title.rendered: BTMS Condenser Airflow: An OEM Installation Review

content.rendered:
The airflow conditions for a Battery Thermal Management System (BTMS) condenser should be evaluated with the unit installed in the vehicle, rather than relying solely on tests conducted on an open test bench. For air-cooled battery cooling systems, cooling performance can be compromised if airflow paths are obstructed or if exhausted hot air recirculates back into the air intake. Before considering a larger-capacity cooler, verify whether the environmental conditions at the condenser’s air intake align with the conditions under which the supplier’s rated capacity was determined.

This guide is intended to assist development teams working on electric buses and trucks in conducting “air-side” installation assessments. It does not prescribe universal requirements for clearances, airflow direction, or fan settings; specific details must be verified against the technical drawings and installation requirements provided by the equipment manufacturer.

Measure the actual air conditions at the intake, rather than relying solely on ambient temperature data from a weather station.

The ambient temperature signal reported by the vehicle may not accurately reflect the conditions of the air entering the condenser. Nearby heat sources or exhaust airflow can alter local environmental conditions. Before positioning sensors, consult the supplier’s drawings to precisely identify the air intake and exhaust locations; observing the fan from the side is not a reliable method for determining airflow direction.

During comparative testing in the development phase, record both the external reference air temperature and the temperatures at several representative intake locations. The reference sensor should be placed away from the unit’s exhaust and any other heat sources; additionally, the sensor’s shielding status and exact installation location must be documented. If a consistent temperature differential is observed between the intake air and the reference temperature, this should be treated as an indicator that the installation requires further investigation, rather than being immediately classified as a specific fault or a breach of a universal failure threshold.

Eaton’s maintenance guidelines for cooling units emphasize critical “air-side” factors, such as proper ventilation, the cleanliness of the condenser fins, and the prevention of hot-air recirculation. Please note, however, that the specific clearance requirements and maintenance instructions provided in those product-specific guidelines do not constitute the official EVLINK vehicle installation specifications.

Conduct a comprehensive assessment of the airflow paths within the vehicle’s installation compartment.

Indicate the intended locations for air inlets, heat exchanger airflow paths, and air outlets on the vehicle layout drawing. Evaluations must be conducted with all body panels, protective guards, wiring harnesses, and peripheral equipment fully installed. Relying solely on visual inspection in an open workshop environment is insufficient to ensure that the airflow paths within the final enclosure meet the required specifications.

  • Air Inlets: Inspect surrounding body panels, grille openings, and areas prone to the accumulation of debris or foreign matter.
  • Air Outlets: Clearly define the exhaust path for hot air and verify that it does not recirculate back into the air inlets.
  • Additional Components: If air ducts, filters, or sound-insulating devices are included, submit them to the supplier for evaluation to determine their impact on pressure drop and the fan’s operating point.
  • Maintenance Access: Ensure sufficient space is provided for service, inspection, and cleaning procedures.

Do not simply adopt clearance requirements from manuals for other types of chillers. While YORK installation guides explain the effects of airflow obstruction and recirculation, the specific dimensions and fan limitations provided therein apply only to chillers designed for building HVAC applications. Always obtain the specific limits applicable to your unique Battery Thermal Management System (BTMS) configuration.

Distinguishing Between “Airflow Obstruction” and “Airflow Recirculation”

While these two phenomena can occur simultaneously, they are defined by different criteria. A grille may obstruct an airflow path without necessarily causing a significant rise in intake air temperature; conversely, even if an opening appears sufficiently large, airflow recirculation can still occur, leading to an increase in intake air temperature. It is not possible to accurately assess the actual airflow through an installed heat exchanger based solely on fan control commands or the sound produced by the fan.

Use a comparative test procedure approved by the supplier. During testing, ensure that cooling demands, coolant conditions, and vehicle operating states remain as consistent as possible. Compare the proposed production configuration against an approved development reference configuration, adjusting only one layout (packaging) variable at a time. Document variations in load, airflow conditions, and initial temperatures; do not treat tests conducted under different operating conditions as controlled experiments.

Testing with panels removed helps isolate the effects of the packaging (layout), but such results cannot serve as the basis for mass-production acceptance. Any alternative panel or ducting configuration must be verified to ensure it meets all structural and electrical safety requirements. Personnel must strictly adhere to established isolation and operational protocols; it is strictly prohibited to remove protective guards, expose live electrical components, or bypass safety measures while fans are in operation.

Collect data from both the air side and the coolant side in a time-synchronized manner.

The following recommendations are for reference only; they do not constitute mandatory standards and cannot replace a supplier’s own validation plan:

  • Vehicle state (e.g., stationary, charging, or driving); record the associated load, airflow conditions, and panel configuration.
  • Reference air temperature and representative temperature at the condenser inlet (specify sensor locations).
  • Cooling demand, fan commands, and fan feedback; compressor status and any reported faults.
  • Coolant inlet/outlet temperatures and flow rates measured at defined boundaries.
  • Time-synchronized battery pack temperature data, initial conditions, and duration of operation.

These signals help distinguish between “air-side packaging issues” and “coolant distribution or control issues.” If responses vary across different areas of the battery pack, refer to the diagnostic guidelines for coolant flow distribution and temperature profiling within the Battery Thermal Management System (BTMS). A high reading from a single sensor or an increased fan demand is not sufficient, on its own, to determine the root cause.

Reach a consensus on validation evidence before finalizing the packaging configuration.

Provide the supplier with a detailed layout drawing of the compartment, specifying inlet/outlet locations, grille or ducting details, adjacent heat sources, installation photographs, and the required operating conditions. Require the supplier to provide written confirmation of clearance requirements, allowable increases in air-side resistance, service/maintenance access space, and rated capacity operating conditions for the specific vehicle model. If any data is missing, document it as an open engineering item; do not simply insert generic values.

Incorporate relevant static operating conditions into the agreed-upon test plan—for example, during the charging process or while the vehicle is stationary following a period of high-load operation. Good performance under driving conditions does not guarantee that the system will meet requirements under other static conditions. Acceptance criteria should be based on the OEM’s battery boundary conditions and the supplier’s specified operating range; furthermore, all testing must be conducted using approved, production-intent panels.

Points for discussion with the BTMS supplier:

Can airflow issues be resolved by installing a larger fan?

A fan should not be replaced without a formal assessment. The supplier must evaluate the entire airflow path, considering the operating point of the proposed fan, electrical requirements, control compatibility, and installation constraints. Simply increasing the fan’s rated specifications does not guarantee that the condenser will receive the required airflow within the vehicle’s actual packaging layout.

Should grilles or filters be permanently removed?

Temporary adjustments made during the diagnostic process should not be automatically adopted as production decisions. Grilles, filters, and panels may serve other essential functions. Any proposed changes must be validated, taking into account airflow dynamics, protective measures, contamination prevention, noise control, and maintenance requirements.

What clearance (spacing) should be provided?

Refer to the requirements published by your chosen Battery Thermal Management System (BTMS) supplier and verify them against the specific installation location on the vehicle. This guide does not prescribe a universal clearance standard. During the planning phase, ensure there is sufficient space for necessary maintenance tasks while also guaranteeing unobstructed airflow.

Prepare an EVLINK installation assessment summary

When engaging with EVLINK on a project, please provide the vehicle’s installation layout, expected cooling loads, ambient intake conditions, coolant requirements, and the proposed grille or ducting configuration. This will establish a clear starting point for engineering discussions, ensuring thorough alignment before a final configuration is selected.

Submit your layout proposal and operating conditions to EVLINK. Please clearly distinguish between parameters or test conditions that are already finalized and those that remain to be confirmed; this allows the assessment process to focus on items that still require decision-making.
